title: Visit the sick
hookLine: I was sick and you visited me
tomorrow: why doesn't the king ask what the prisoner did?

cards: Fourth floor. The elevator opens on that smell, hand sanitizer and cafeteria gravy. Room 412: the TV on mute, a pudding cup nobody opened, a balloon already sagging.
In the bed is someone you love, smaller than you remember. And there you are in the doorway with empty hands. No flowers.
No wise words. Nothing that fixes anything. It's tempting to say something useful fast, or to leave.
So what is a person in that doorway actually for?

teach.b: Jesus answers it in a story about the end of time. A king sorts the nations like a shepherd sorting sheep from goats, and tells the blessed why they're welcome.
One reason, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "sick, and you visited me." Look at the verb. Not healed.
Not cured. Visited. The just in the story brought no miracle.

teach.h: WHEN DID WE SEE YOU SICK?
teach.b: And they're surprised: when did we see you sick?

The king says what they did for the least of his brethren, they did for him. Now a detail worth repeating tonight. In Luke's Gospel, old Zachary holds his newborn son and blesses God because "he hath visited" his people.
In Greek, that's the same verb as the king's. The word for God coming close is the word for a chair pulled up to a bed. The Church kept the two together.
The Catechism names visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy, the mercies for the body. The book of Sirach, in Catholic Bibles, says not to be slow to visit the sick.
And the letter of James tells the sick to call in the priests to pray over them and anoint them with oil; Catholics see in it the anointing of the sick. A visit needs no training at all.

teach.h: A CARD, A CALL, A CHAIR.
teach.b: A card, a call, half an hour in a plastic chair.
In the doorway, the job is to come in.

how: Catholic priests anoint the seriously ill, lay ministers bring Communion to people at home and in hospitals, and some parishes organize volunteers to visit the homebound.

o: work as a nurse at a Catholic hospital
spend time with someone who is ill
pray for healing at a holy shrine

games.q: who's in the story — tap the pairs.
p: surprised: when did we see you sick?
blessed God, who visited his people
call the priests to pray and anoint

s: the anointing of the sick is only for people about to die
the Church offers it to the seriously ill, not only at the very end.
in Matthew 25 the just are praised for healing the sick
the king says visited. nobody in the story cures anyone; they came.
the just didn't know it was the king they had visited
they ask, when did we see you sick? that's the surprise of the story.

games.q: a teammate's mom is home after surgery. you have ten minutes after practice and nothing clever to say. what fits the king's words best?
o: stop by for ten minutes, sit with her, and ask nothing hard.
read up on her surgery first so you can give real advice.
wait until she's fully better so you don't bother her.
games.why: the king praises the visit, not the cure or the advice, and Sirach says not to be slow about it. a short visit still counts.

practice: This one uses your phone. Bring to mind someone who is sick, healing, or stuck at home, and send them a short message that asks nothing back: no question to answer, no advice.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name as it sends; if not, let them be the one you hold in mind for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Visit the sick. A work of mercy that's mostly showing up: a door, a chair, some time.

orig.note: Greek: you visited. the king's word in Matthew 25:36, and Luke's verb for God visiting his people.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: you visited me, not you healed me or you fixed me. Take care.

sources.ref: CCC 2447 (works of mercy); CCC 1510–1514 (anointing of the sick)
